summary: This note is a short Wikipedia-style biographical entry on Manfredo Tafuri, an Italian architect, historian, theoretician, critic and academic who lived from 1935 to 1994. One commentator called him the world's most important architectural historian of the second half of the 20th century. The note highlights his critiques of the partisan 'operative criticism' of Bruno Zevi and Siegfried Giedion, and his challenge to the view of the Renaissance as a 'golden age' held by Heinrich Wölfflin and Rudolf Wittkower.
one_line: Biographical entry on Manfredo Tafuri, Italian architectural historian and critic known for challenging operative criticism and Renaissance idealisation.
key_facts: Manfredo Tafuri was born in Rome on 4 November 1935.
Manfredo Tafuri died in Venice on 23 February 1994.
Manfredo Tafuri was an Italian architect, historian, theoretician, critic and academic.
One commentator described Manfredo Tafuri as the world's most important architectural historian of the second half of the 20th century.
Manfredo Tafuri is noted for pointed critiques of the partisan "operative criticism" of previous architectural historians and critics.
Bruno Zevi is named as one of the critics whose operative criticism Manfredo Tafuri critiqued.
Siegfried Giedion is named as one of the critics whose operative criticism Manfredo Tafuri critiqued.
Manfredo Tafuri challenged the idea that the Renaissance was a "golden age".
The Renaissance was characterised as a "golden age" in the work of earlier authorities such as Heinrich Wölfflin.
The Renaissance was characterised as a "golden age" in the work of earlier authorities such as Rudolf Wittkower.
